content: The number of platelet apheresis donations recorded was 132,275, while the number of granulocyte apheresis donations was 14. Plasma apheresis donations, amounting to 139 liters, were not included in the aforementioned figures. In 2011, the United Republic of Tanzania reported no apheresis blood donations. Similarly, no data was reported for 2012 and 2013. In contrast, the United States of America reported 197,800 apheresis donations in 2011, with no pre-deposit autologous blood donations recorded. By 2012, the USA reported 110,042 apheresis donations, with 71 from first-time donors and 408 from repeat donors. In 2013, the USA recorded 102,732 apheresis donations, with 55 from first-time donors and 880 from repeat donors. Uruguay reported 408 apheresis donations in 2012 and 1,121 in 2013. Uzbekistan did not report any data for 2011, 2012, or 2013. Vanuatu reported no apheresis donations in 2011 and 2013, with no data available for 2012. Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of) did not provide data for 2011, 2012, or 2013. Viet Nam reported 492 apheresis donations in 2011, 535 in 2012, and 470 in 2013. Yemen did not report any data for 2011, 2012, or 2013. Zambia reported 192 apheresis donations in 2011, 8 in 2012, and 20 in 2013. Zimbabwe reported 160 apheresis donations in 2011, 107 in 2012, and 15 in 2013. In 2013, laboratory testing requirements for screening donated blood for transfusion-transmissible infections (TTIs) were mandatory in many countries. For example, Afghanistan required testing for HIV 1+2, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and syphilis. Algeria also mandated testing for these infections, along with additional tests for Chagas disease and malaria. Angola required testing for HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, syphilis, Chagas disease, malaria, and HTLV I/II. Argentina required testing for HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, syphilis, Chagas disease, malaria, and HTLV I/II, among others. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, blood testing was centralized at three levels: the National Blood Transfusion Centre (CNTS), provincial blood transfusion centers (CPTS), and hospital blood banks (CHRTS). Testing included HIV, Hepatitis B and C, syphilis, and blood grouping, conducted twice a year. Samples were sent to the national laboratory for retesting. In 2013, the number of blood centers performing laboratory screening for TTIs varied by country. For example, Afghanistan had 14 centers, Albania had 10, and Algeria had 200. In contrast, some countries, such as Andorra and Azerbaijan, did not report any data. In the United States, 22 blood centers performed laboratory screening for TTIs in 2013. In Nepal, all testing laboratories participated in the national external quality assessment scheme (EQAS) for HIV. Two services participated in international EQAS for all TTIs, and 33 services participated in the national EQAS for syphilis. The Central Blood Transfusion Service regularly participated in the EQAS system with NRL Australia. Hospital blood transfusion units in the Kathmandu Valley participated in the EQAS system run by the National Public Health Laboratory of the Nepal Government. In Rwanda, TTI testing was centralized in the national center. In Serbia, the Blood Transfusion Institute, which collected, tested, and processed approximately 40% of the country's blood, was the only laboratory participating in EQAS for TTIs in 2011. By 2013, three regional blood centers participated in EQAS for TTIs. In Viet Nam, the number of blood centers performing laboratory screening for TTIs increased from 67 in 2011 to 72 in 2013. In Zambia, 99 blood centers performed laboratory screening for TTIs consistently from 2011 to 2013.
